paras: The lynching of Frank Easterling took place on the night of Saturday, October 6, 1888, in Rankin County, Mississippi, when a mob took Easterling, a Black man, out and hanged him and shot Sharper Easterling, at whose house he was found. Mississippi papers gave two motives: the first reports said Frank was killed for saying he would vote Democratic, while later briefs said he was accused of stealing cotton.

According to a dispatch dated Brandon, October 8, Frank Easterling lived in Rankin County and had declared on the streets of Brandon the previous Wednesday that he intended to vote the Democratic ticket in November. The Chickasaw Messenger of Okolona instead said that Frank's offense was stealing cotton, and that Sharp Easterling had been charged with harboring him after vigilantes notified Sharp to leave.

On Saturday night a mob took Frank Easterling out and hanged him. The same mob that night shot Sharper Easterling, described in the Brandon dispatch as "a negro Democrat" at whose house Frank was found. The dispatch said Sharper was expected to die, but no later report of his condition appears in the coverage.

The attackers were described only as a "mob," "vigilantes," or "unknown persons," and the Pascagoula Democrat-Star noted that their race was not stated. No report of an arrest, inquest, or grand jury action was found.

The story ran only in Mississippi weeklies, and the first versions were partisan. The Brookhaven Leader printed the Brandon dispatch under the headline "Killed for Being a Democrat-- Carry the News to Chandler and John Sherman," pointing the news at Northern Republicans. The Pascagoula Democrat-Star wrote that "colored Democrats are not safe in Rankin county" and, while admitting the slayers' race was unknown, called them "carpetbaggers, scalawags or negroes" and "ultra Republicans."

A week later the tone changed. The Brookhaven Leader's state-news column called Frank "a notoriously bad character" and said Sharp was shot for harboring him, with a sentence beginning "Polites had nothing to do" that breaks off in the surviving text. The Chickasaw Messenger said that in its own section such a case would go to the grand jury and that Sharp's conduct was no crime, then turned the episode against Governor Lowry, whose home was in Rankin, remarking that "the wonder is that more people are not lynched in that locality."

The motive is disputed: the Brandon dispatch and the Democrat-Star said the men were attacked for being Democrats, while the later briefs blamed theft and the harboring of a thief. The political version came first and from a Brandon dateline, but none of the reports names its source.

reader.title: Lynching of Frank Easterling
bases: A mob took Frank Easterling out at night and hanged him and shot the man at whose house he was found (A1, A2); later items describe both as 'mobbed' (A3, A4).

Two reports say a mob hanged Frank Easterling (A1, A2), and no report denies his death, though the later briefs say only 'mobbed' (A3, A4); the killers were a 'mob' or 'vigilantes' acting without authority, and the Okolona editorial gives a pretext of cotton theft (A4), while the first reports give a political motive (A1, A2).

Four items in three Mississippi papers agree that a mob attacked Frank and Sharp Easterling in Rankin County (A1, A2, A3, A4), though they disagree on the motive and A2 may rest on the same dispatch as A1.

accounts.label: Brandon dispatch (political motive)
accounts.gist: Frank Easterling was hanged by a mob after saying he would vote Democratic, and Sharper Easterling, 'a negro Democrat', was shot at his house the same night.

accounts.label: Later state briefs (theft and harboring)
accounts.gist: Frank was a thief or 'notoriously bad character' accused of stealing cotton, and Sharp was shot for harboring him after vigilantes had told him to leave.

framing.detail: The Brookhaven Leader headed the dispatch 'Killed for Being a Democrat-- Carry the News to Chandler and John Sherman', turning the killing against Northern Republicans.
The Pascagoula Democrat-Star said 'colored Democrats are not safe in Rankin county' and blamed 'carpetbaggers, scalawags or negroes', while noting the slayers' race was not stated.
The Brookhaven Leader's later brief called Frank 'a notoriously bad character' and appears to deny a political motive.
The Chickasaw Messenger said such cases belonged before the grand jury and that Sharp had committed no crime, but aimed its sarcasm at Gov. Lowry and the Brandon Republican.
